analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for executive pay above 25 times a company's lowest worker's pay.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 7 House Democrats behind it, never got a hearing or a vote in the Ways and Means Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop companies from deducting from their taxes any employee's pay that exceeds the greater of 25 times what their lowest-paid full-time worker earns or $500,000. It counts every form of pay — salary, bonus, stock options, retirement contributions — and would require companies that pay top employees more than 25 times their lowest wage to report the pay gap to the Treasury. Companies could still pay executives whatever they want; they would just lose the tax write-off on the excess.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, because corporations would no longer reduce their tax bills by writing off multimillion-dollar executive pay packages. It would also give companies a tax reason to raise their lowest wages, since raising the bottom raises the ceiling for deductible top pay. The public reporting requirement would let workers and investors see the pay gaps inside large companies.

how_it_helps.text: Denies a tax deduction for compensation above the greater of 25 times a company's lowest-paid full-time employee or $500,000, covering salary, bonuses, options, retirement contributions, and other pay [S2][S3].

Requires any employer paying someone more than 25 times its lowest-paid worker to report that worker's pay, average non-managerial pay, average executive pay, and the exact pay of its top 5 employees to the Treasury [S3].
Defines employer to include all companies under common ownership or control, so pay could not be hidden by splitting a business into affiliated companies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and their highest-paid executives, who would lose a tax write-off worth hundreds of millions of dollars industry-wide. Companies could avoid the limit by narrowing their internal pay gaps or by raising their lowest wages — which is the point — but any company wanting to keep both extreme executive pay and the deduction would pay more tax.

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise only a modest amount of revenue and does not directly raise any worker's pay; a company determined to pay an executive $20 million simply pays more tax, and nothing in the bill forces that money to workers [S2][S3].

The reporting requirement adds a compliance burden, and firms could restructure pay into forms or timing that are harder to count, though the bill gives Treasury authority to sweep in other forms of compensation [S3].

A good-faith objection is that pay ratios are a blunt tool: a small firm where the owner earns far more than a first hire, or a firm with few low-wage employees, faces different realities than a giant retailer — the bill addresses this with the $500,000 floor, but edge cases remain [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: it closes a tax write-off that rewards the widest pay gaps and nudges companies toward raising bottom wages rather than top pay. It is not a wage mandate and would not by itself close any gap. The main cost falls on shareholders and executives through higher corporate tax bills, and the honest case against it is that it targets a symptom — extreme pay ratios — with a tax rule rather than directly raising anyone's wages.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee of California introduced the bill on January 20, 2011, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
Six Democratic colleagues cosponsored it; no Republican did [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and their highest-paid executives kept the tax deduction for outsized pay packages, and no company had to narrow its pay gaps or file the pay-gap report.

sides.party_line_note: All 7 supporters were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-led Ways and Means Committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: They would lose the tax deduction on executive pay above 25 times their lowest wage or $500,000, whichever is larger, and would have to file pay-gap reports with the Treasury. The deduction they keep today effectively lets the public share the cost of outsized executive pay.

industries.industry: Top executives and the highest-earning employees
industries.note: Their pay packages would no longer be partially paid for by a tax write-off, giving boards a tax reason to either raise the lowest wages or rein in top pay. All forms of pay — options, bonuses, deferred compensation, retirement contributions — count against the cap.
Higher corporate tax bills would cut after-tax earnings slightly, but investors also gain from the required disclosure of pay gaps, which research links to weaker company performance.
